stories.title_en: Luring Him into Drink and Whoring to Ruin His Life and Name

paragraphs.en: Shi Juan was a native of Macheng in Huguang. Rich and full of deceit, he was touchy and hated to lose. He had once clashed with his elder cousin Shi Jian over rival bids for fields and houses, and bad blood remained between them. Jian’s son Shi Xiao studied, won a place in the county school, and was handsome, quick-witted, and a gifted writer; many predicted he would pass the examinations. Shi Juan nursed his jealousy: “All my life I have made money, yet brother Jian has always kept me in his shadow. Now his son has joined the ranks of the scholars—a tiger grown wings.” So he cast about for a scheme to wound Jian and Xiao, father and son, in secret.

A few years later Jian died. Shi Xiao was in mourning, with no one to keep him in line. Juan thought: Xiao is young and unbridled; perhaps he can be baited with wine and women. So he feigned friendship and attached himself to the boy: where Xiao went, Juan went; whatever Xiao approved, Juan approved. They spent whole days chasing amusements together and made merry over wine again and again. Whenever a pretty courtesan appeared, Juan invited Xiao to drink at her house; whenever a good actress came to town, Juan would stage a play and invite Xiao to drink, telling the actress to fawn on him with every art, bent on stirring his lust. Xiao fell into the trap without knowing it. He idled away the months and let his books go to waste. When the mourning ended and he sat the make-up examination, he was placed in the bottom grade. Xiao then roused himself and went to study at a temple, but Juan would drag along friends and courtesans, carting wine to the temple for drinking bouts. At the sight of the courtesans Xiao’s heart lifted despite himself, and his old habits sprouted again. Juan next urged Xiao to take two beautiful concubines, and he wallowed in lust morning and night. Wasted by sex within and soaked in wine without, his hands were seized with a tremor and he could no longer write a steady hand. At the circuit examination he was struck off the rolls, and the family estate withered. Shi Juan clapped and roared with laughter: “The grudge of a lifetime is vented, and my scheme has succeeded!” Then he called his sons and lectured them: “While brother Jian lived, his house was richer than mine. But he sired that worthless Xiao, whose one love was drinking and whoring and who would not touch his books, so he threw away his future and ended up a homeless dog. Take him as a warning, and never follow in his ruts.” Not long after, his own sons were led by others into gambling and whoring, and the money they burned through was beyond counting. Juan was old by then and could do nothing; he could only heave long sighs.

Note: Shi Juan had a hundred crafty tricks. He hid an old grudge and made friends with Xiao, and drowned him in wine and lust until his name and his fortune were both lost. Juan thought he had won and could vent his long-held spite; it never crossed his mind that if you kill a man’s father, others will kill yours, and if you kill a man’s brother, others will kill yours. Heaven’s net is vast, and its reckoning never errs. How could he be sure no one else would borrow his old trick, or that his own sons and grandsons would not follow the same ruts? The warning he gave his two sons was a far cry from a righteous father’s teaching—so why be surprised that his sons went the same way? And yet Xiao was a fool too. Had he possessed an ounce of sense, he should have reckoned: while my father lived, this man was his enemy; now that my father is gone, the most I can ask is that he let the grudge go—how could I expect friendship that deep? That something unfathomable lay behind it should have been plain. If Xiao had taken sloth and debauchery as his warning and driven himself on without rest, then however crafty Shi Juan was, how could he have struck a man who stood on his own feet?

stories.title_en: Luring a Friend into Adultery to Take His Land

paragraphs.en: Bi He was a native of Shanxi, sly and ruthless at heart, vicious and poisonous in secret; there was no one in the village he had not harmed. His younger cousin Bi Song owned a stretch of land worth more than fifty taels, right next to He’s fields. He had schemed for it time and again without success, so he feigned friendship instead: he feasted Song again and again and kept him company from morning to night, as close as any blood brother.

In the same village lived a man named Lin Yuan, hard and violent by nature. His wife, born Luo, was beautiful and loose, and she and her husband were at odds. He seized the opening and seduced her; they began an affair and grew very close. He pretended to keep it from Song while in fact wanting Song to find out—half hiding it, half letting it show—until Song saw through him. Song reproached him: “So much for our friendship. With a beauty like that, why not take me along for a night? Do you think I would steal her from you?” He answered with a show of deference: “The woman is full of feeling. If I brought you, she would surely dote on you. But I fear you would come and go without restraint, word would leak out, and if her husband found out, it could cost you your family and your neck.” Song only suspected He of keeping her all to himself, so he went on his own to seduce her, and Luo gave in. After that the affair grew still more tangled: whenever the husband was out, if it was not He who went, it was Song; at times all three even shared one bed, close as a single body.

When nearly a month had passed, He secretly tipped off the husband: “Song is my dearest friend, but now I hear he is carrying on with your wife. I have warned him again and again and he will not listen. I hear you mean to catch them. If you do, give him only a light beating. He is sure to call me in to mediate, and I will make him pay you a good sum of silver to put an end to his mischief. Whatever you do, do not take his life.” Lin Yuan heard this and rage filled his chest. The next day he announced he was going out and would not be back for three days. Song had been watching for Yuan’s departure; the moment he heard the man was away, he went to the house, pulled Luo into the bedroom, and began to fool around. Lin Yuan burst out of hiding and charged into the room, where the two had already undressed on the bed. Yuan hauled Song off the bed and beat him savagely; Luo threw herself on her husband’s arms with all her strength, so Yuan could not land many blows. Song begged for release: “Let me buy my way out with silver.” Yuan said: “Who will stand surety for you?” Song said: “Fetch my cousin He.” That was exactly what Yuan wanted, and he sent for He at once. He said: “You strayed from the straight path, and it has come to this. We must call your own elder brother.” Song said: “Don’t call my brother. Just put up the silver for me and I will pay you back in a few days.” He said: “I came to mediate—how can I be the one paying? But the matter is urgent. If I do not put up the silver, there is no way out of this. Still, there must be real property to match it.” So Song wrote out a deed selling He the adjoining field. He said: “You can only price it low; any more would just end up in Lin Yuan’s pocket.” They set the price at a mere forty taels. He went home, brought back thirty taels, and handed them over. Yuan said: “I want sixty.” He said: “For adultery caught in the act, the forfeit is half the wife’s value. Even granting your wife is a beauty worth sixty taels, this is already half.” Yuan refused again and again. He said: “His field is priced at forty taels, and I have no more ready silver on hand. Better to agree that a month from now he collects another ten taels from me.” Yuan demanded a written pledge. He said: “If anyone else had mediated, he would take a twenty percent cut—I would already be owed eight taels. Here I am settling your affair for nothing, and you press me for a note?” So no note was written, and He took Song home with him.

A few days later Song brought principal and interest—forty-four taels—to redeem the field, but He refused to give it back. A month later Lin Yuan came to He for the promised silver. He said: “I showed you how to pocket thirty taels; is two taels in thanks too much to ask?” Yuan later told others how He had put him up to catching the adulterers, and only then did Song learn that He had sold him out. But he had already fallen into the trap, and regret came too late.

Note: He wanted Song’s field, so first he led him into adultery; and to lead him into adultery, he first made himself Song’s friend. Nor did he openly push Song into the affair—he let Song walk into it on his own. And in claiming the field, he waited for Song’s hour of desperation, then ‘settled the quarrel’ for him and gathered it in at his leisure. A clever scheme indeed. Had it not been for the silver promised afterward, Lin Yuan would never have revealed how it began, and who could have fathomed the depth of He’s devotion—or the depth of his poison? So when a man’s conduct is venomous and crooked, then however close he is to you, you must keep your guard up.

stories.title_en: Piling Up a Friend’s Debts to Ruin His House

paragraphs.en: Jin Congyu and Hong Qiyu were both men of Yingtian Prefecture. Their shops stood a dozen or so doors apart, and both ran large stores dealing in goods from the capital, each with capital of more than a thousand taels. But Congyu was sly and ruthless, while Qiyu was gentle, honest, and simple. Both often went to buy capital goods and met again and again at feasts; each could hold his wine, and they toasted one another merrily.

Congyu thought: “As the saying goes, the kind cannot command troops and the upright cannot hold on to money. I see that Qiyu is charitable and fond of doing good, honest and without guile. Why should his shop’s trade rival mine? I must snare him with craft.” So he feigned close friendship: he sent gifts at every season, and whenever there was a celebration he invited Qiyu. Qiyu took Jin’s attentions as goodwill and always returned small gifts with generous ones. Congyu said: “The man loves wine; wine will be his ruin.” So he kept up a round of monthly blessing feasts, split-the-bill dinners, and guild celebrations—there was hardly a day without a drinking invitation. On fine days with lovely views he took Qiyu roaming; on cool moonlit nights they talked in private until dawn. Qiyu duly fell for the trap: he spent his days in a drunken haze and gave no thought to business. Congyu might spend his days drinking and roaming with Qiyu, but he had a younger brother, Jiyu, in the shop who could manage everything. Qiyu idled away his time while his own shop stood empty and unwatched. Customers who came looking for him and found him gone mostly went to buy at Jiyu’s shop instead. So Jin’s shop flourished by the day while Hong’s declined by the day, and Qiyu gradually ran short of funds. Congyu gave him money whenever he asked—but each time half of it was ninety-percent silver and half only seventy or eighty, and the weight came up light on the scale. He never asked for a loan note, only saying, “Just keep a clear account.” In less than four or five years the loans had mounted to more than six hundred taels. Then he sent Jiyu to collect. Qiyu borrowed two hundred taels elsewhere to repay, and when the accounts were settled he still owed more than four hundred. They pressed him to sign over his fields and houses as a mortgage—Qiyu meaning to repay the debt later and redeem the land. Qiyu went along with everything they said. Two more years passed, and principal and interest together came to more than four hundred fifty taels. Jiyu pressed hard to collect in full. Qiyu begged Congyu for a little leniency. Congyu said: “My silver is held in common with my younger brother. At home he has often complained that I should never have lent it to you. I will stay out of it now—settle it between the two of you.” By then the Jin household held the freshly written mortgage deed. Qiyu could stall no longer and had to sign over every property he owned to cover the debt. His other creditors, seeing him ruined, all came pressing for payment. A household worth more than a thousand taels was emptied in a stroke within two or three years. It was all the work of Jin Congyu’s entrapment and compounded scheming.

Once Hong’s house was broken, Congyu would not spare him a glance; even if he begged to borrow a single cash, not a hair was given. Congyu then worked the same trick on the son of the Yang shop. Those who saw through it laughed at young Yang: “You are Hong Qiyu’s replacement—why not learn from the cart that overturned ahead of you?” Yang gradually drew away and cut him off.

Note: Lending silver at interest is not, in itself, a compounded swindle. The point is that Hong was a rich merchant to begin with, and Congyu lured him into roaming and drinking until he abandoned his trade and his capital melted away—and only then lent him the silver. Along the way he counted eight as ten, charged thirty percent interest, shorted him on the land price, and nibbled him down like a silkworm on a leaf. Congyu’s treachery and greed knew no limit. Wealth without humanity—what defense can a man like Congyu possibly offer?

stories.title_en: Goading a Friend into an Adultery Suit to Ruin His House

paragraphs.en: Ma Ziming was a native of Shaoxing in Zhejiang—a small-minded schemer, smooth and fawning and full of guile. His younger cousin Ma Ying was flighty and dull, and his household was even richer than Ziming’s. Ying’s father had long been at odds with Ziming’s father; each side was plotting against the other, but neither had struck. Ziming saw that Ying was a fool and a drunk besides, so he drank with him constantly, sometimes rounding up others to split the bill. But only these two formed a real bond; everyone else grew sick of them and would not drink with them. So the two poured for each other, sang each other’s praises, and called themselves bosom friends. Whenever Ying had business, he mostly let Ziming decide, and Ziming would offer little schemes from time to time to prove his devotion. Ying had long been on bad terms with his own elder brother; he often aired the man’s faults and wanted to file a complaint against him. Ziming made a show of talking him out of it, but at the decisive moment he would say just the opposite to provoke him, and Ying’s anger deepened. Ying went ahead and accused his brother first. The officials saw the case clearly and found Ying guilty of assaulting an elder brother; he got off only by calling in favors. This was the beginning of the family’s ruin. After that Ziming egged him into lawsuit after lawsuit, and the household crumbled by the day.

Later Ziming went to a humble household to collect a debt and saw that the wife was young and beautiful. He came home and boasted to Ying: “Today I went to such-and-such a house to collect a debt. The daughter-in-law is a rare beauty, a veritable Xi Shi among women. I made eyes at her and she passed with her head bowed. The house is only one bay wide, so I strolled back and forth in front of it several times. My soul went adrift and I could not help myself. Then I teased her with laughing words, and she answered with a smile—she seemed there for the taking. My only fear was that her husband and his mother would be in the way, so I dared not act. I have been pining for her ever since, waking and sleeping.” Ying said: “That household is one of my tithing heads (jiashou), and they are my tenants besides. What is hard about having her? I will take her first.” Ziming provoked him: “If you can have her, I will stand you a grand feast. But take my advice: do not provoke that dolt of a husband. If he catches you, those coarse fists of his will beat you to death for real.” Ying said: “I have never heard of a tenant daring to lay a hand on his landlord.” The next day he went to the house to collect the consolidated tax. The moment he saw the wife he began teasing her, and sent her mother-in-law out: “Go find some vegetables for lunch.” As soon as the old woman left, he seized the wife and dragged her into the bedroom. She wavered between yielding and refusing; then she saw a woman next door peek in and duck away. She pointed: “Auntie next door saw us—you mustn’t.” He would not stop, taking it for a mere excuse. They had been grappling for a good while when the old woman came back. The wife could only cry out, “Mother! The master is forcing himself on me!” The old woman flared up and scolded him. Enraged, Ying went straight to the county and filed a complaint that the household had defaulted on the consolidated tax, and even accused them of assaulting the village head (lizhang). The tenant in turn accused Ying of rape, and the officials arrested the parties for trial. The neighbor woman had seen it, and the wife’s own mother-in-law had caught them. The wife was, moreover, a city-toppling beauty; the whole courtroom crowded in to stare, clucking in admiration. The case was tried as rape, and Ying was sentenced to death. Later he called in favors and had the charge reduced to seduction in sport, not consummated. But the family estate was ruined; the fields and houses were all sold to Ziming. And Ziming had the gall to scold him: “I told you at the start not to do it. You would not listen, and it has come to this.” Ying said: “Your mouth told me not to, but you had already built the bridge and walked me out onto it—there was no turning back. I want to blame you, yet I cannot quite pin it on you. Mencius said, ‘Condemn him and there is nothing to cite; censure him and there is nothing to seize.’ That is exactly a man like you.”

Once the land was all sold, Ziming cut off all dealings with him. Ying had to beg loans morning and night, and in the end only his own elder brother would take him in. Only then did he learn that blood is blood after all, and that his wine-and-meat friend had been false from the start.

Note: Ying was snared by Ziming; his house was broken and every bit of his property gathered into Ziming’s hands, yet he had taken the man for a bosom friend. What folly! A man of any sense, living in the world, cannot do without brothers, uncles, and nephews within the family, nor without friends and kin beyond it. To sue his own brother while courting the intimacy of a friend is to slight those he should hold dear and hold dear the one he should slight. Consider Sun Hua of old, who cast out his brother Sun Rong and clung to his friends instead: had his wife Lady Yang not been a woman of such virtue, he would have been slow indeed to repent. If a man can take warning and make himself new, then however many clever tricks they have, how could they ever strike a man who has made himself new?
